headline: Stocks slip as Fed officials signal higher-for-longer rates
body: US equities fell on Tuesday after two Federal Reserve officials said the central bank was in no hurry to cut interest rates. The S&P 500 dropped 0.8% and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.1%. The US 10-year Treasury yield rose 0.9 basis points to 4.995% as traders pushed back expectations for easing.

headline: PBOC cuts reserve requirements to support growth
body: The People's Bank of China cut the reserve requirement ratio for major banks by 25 basis points, its first reduction this year. The Shanghai Composite rose 0.9% and the Hang Seng gained 1.4% on the news. The PBOC said the move would release long-term liquidity to support credit growth.

headline: Eurozone inflation eases, lifting European shares
body: Eurozone consumer price inflation slowed to 2.1% in October from 2.3% in September, matching forecasts. The STOXX Europe 600 rose 0.6% and the DAX 40 added 0.8%. The European Central Bank is expected to keep its deposit rate unchanged at its next meeting.

headline: Brazil central bank holds Selic rate at 12.25%
body: Brazil's central bank kept its benchmark Selic rate at 12.25% for a third meeting, citing persistent services inflation. The Ibovespa rose 0.3% after the decision. Policymakers said they would remain vigilant and did not signal a cut before December.

headline: Bank of Japan keeps policy rate unchanged
body: The Bank of Japan left its short-term policy rate unchanged at 0.5% and said it would keep assessing wage growth before another hike. The Nikkei 225 fell 0.4% while the yen weakened modestly against the dollar. The Japan 10-year yield was little changed.

headline: OPEC+ extends output cuts, pushing oil higher
body: OPEC+ agreed to extend its voluntary production cuts through the first quarter of next year. Brent crude rose 1.2% to $78.40 a barrel and WTI gained 1.1%. The group said the decision reflected a cautious view of demand.

headline: Nvidia forecasts strong data-center demand
body: Nvidia reported quarterly data-center revenue of $42 billion, above analyst estimates, and guided to further growth next quarter. The company said demand for its AI accelerators remained supply constrained. Nvidia shares rose 3.2% in after-hours trading.

headline: Semiconductor stocks rally on AI spending
body: Semiconductor shares climbed after several cloud providers raised their capital spending forecasts for AI infrastructure. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 2.4%. Analysts said advanced packaging capacity remains the main bottleneck for chipmakers.

headline: Canva announces major job cuts after 'our hardest year yet'
body:
Canva co-founder Melanie Perkins says this year has been "our hardest" yet
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.
In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.
The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.
It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.
The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.
"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."
The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.
Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.
Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.
"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.
Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.
The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.

headline: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?
body:
Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to raise UK interest rates for the first time in more than three years at their next meeting.
Most analysts believe the Bank rate will go up from 3.75% to 4%, following holds at the previous six meetings.
Before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February, rates had been expected to fall this year, but the economic fallout from the conflict has pushed up inflation across the globe.
Interest rates affect mortgage, credit card and savings rates for millions of people.
An interest rate tells you how much it costs to borrow money, or the reward for saving it.
The Bank of England's base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings.
The Bank moves its base rate up and down in order to keep UK inflation — the rate at which prices are increasing — at or near 2%.
When inflation is above that target, the Bank typically puts rates up.
The idea is to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises.
The Bank of England's base rate rose to 5.25% in August 2023. It remained at that level until August 2024, when the Bank started cutting.
Five cuts brought rates down to 4%, before the Bank held rates at its meetings in September and November 2025.
It then cut in December 2025 before holding rates steady in January, March, April, June, July and September 2026.
Meanwhile, the main UK inflation measure, CPI, has fallen significantly since the October 2022 high of 11.1%, which was caused by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
However, the rate has been heading back up and is expected to go higher. It was 3.5% in the year to September 2026 , up from 3.1% the previous month and well above the central bank's 2% target.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS), which tracks UK inflation, blamed the acceleration on sharp rises in petrol and diesel prices.
The US-Israel war with Iran has put up energy and fuel costs around the world, which has increased the pace of price rises more generally.
What is happening to UK prices?
At the start of the year, the Bank had been expected to cut interest rates twice in 2026, with the first drop predicted to come in March or April.
However, the increase in fuel prices and inflation after the outbreak of the conflict has upended all of this. Oil prices initially rose sharply as a result of disruption to supplies in the region, but dropped back when various ceasefires were agreed.
Oil prices rose again when the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July.
UK household energy bills rose after the increases in the price cap in July and October, while global oil prices have risen again recently.
Given the uncertainty, many analysts think UK interest rates will rise at the November meeting and again early next year.
What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?
Why are UK fuel prices rising again?
Just under a third of households have a mortgage, according to the government's English Housing Survey , external .
About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate.
Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost would go up by about £31 a month if the Bank raises the base rate by 0.25 percentage points, but it depends on the size of people's loans.
An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) would wait to see if their lender chose to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise.
But the vast majority of mortgage customers - some 87% - have fixed-rate deals. While their monthly payments aren't immediately affected by a rate change, their future deals are.
Most lenders have already priced in a rise in the Bank rate in November, so this is already reflected in any rates being offered.
As of 4 November, the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate was at 5.96%, while the average five-year rate stood at 5.99%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.
The average two-year tracker rate was 4.67%.
About 800,000 fixed-rate mortgages with an interest rate of 3% or below are expected to expire every year, on average, until the end of 2027. Borrowing costs for customers coming off those deals are likely to rise sharply.

Bank of England interest rates also influence the amount charged on credit cards, new bank loans and car loans.
Lenders can decide to raise their own interest rates if Bank hikes make borrowing costs more expensive.
Equally, they can cut their own rates if Bank cuts make borrowing cheaper.
The Bank base rate also affects how much savers earn on their money.
A rising base rate is likely to mean an increase in the returns offered to savers by banks and building societies and vice versa.
As of 4 November, Moneyfacts said the average rate for an easy access savings account based on a balance of £10,000 was 2.58%. The average rate for an easy access cash ISA was 2.79%.
The average rate for customers who were prepared to lock their money away for a year was 4.48%.
Changes in rates particularly affect those who rely on the interest from their savings to top up their income.
In recent years, the UK has had one of the highest interest rates in the G7 - the group representing the world's seven largest so-called "advanced" economies.
In June 2024, the European Central Bank (ECB) started cutting the main interest rate for the eurozone from an all-time high of 4%, falling to 2% in June 2025.
However, in June 2026, the ECB raised rates to 2.25% as it reacted to the Iran war, before raising them again to 2.5% in September.
The US central bank - the Federal Reserve - raised rates for the first time in three years at its September meeting , the third under the new chair Kevin Warsh.
It meant rates rose to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75%, following three cuts since September 2025.
US President Donald Trump had repeatedly attacked the previous Fed chair Jerome Powell for not cutting rates.
Warsh said the rise was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision".
After the announcement, Trump expressed support for Warsh but said the Fed board, which votes on rate decisions, was "hostile".

headline: Swim and gym prices set to rise above inflation
body:
Bosses at Perdiswell Leisure Centre in Worcester want to increase its fees from January
Inflation-busting price increases are on the way at a large Worcester leisure centre, with its operators blaming energy and staffing costs.
The price of an adult swim at Perdiswell Leisure Centre could rise 6.8% – from £7.30 to £7.80 – if the new charges are approved.
Fitness class fees would increase by 5.6% to £9.50, while the price of annual memberships would go up 4.9%.
Bosses at Freedom Leisure, the site's operator, said staffing and energy bills were rising faster than income as Worcester City Council were asked to approve the new prices.
A report on the price hikes, which outstrip the UK's 3.6% inflation rate, revealed energy costs had more than doubled in recent years, despite efforts to slash consumption.
If councillors sign them off in a meeting at the end of November, the average fee at Perdiswell Leisure Centre would increase by 5.3% from January.
Matt Wickham, from Freedom Leisure, said things are "tough" for the whole leisure industry
Hiring the artificial pitch at Perdiswell, which can currently be done for £44 an hour, would cost 10% more, although the council said it would still be significantly cheaper than comparable pitches elsewhere in the city.
Matt Wickham, Freedom Leisure's chief operating officer, explained the firm had seen "significant cost increases", with gas prices up by more than 50% over the second half of the year and minimum wages rising year-on-year.
"It's really tough because we know people are feeling the pinch in different ways, but our priority is all about offering a value-for-money service to people from all walks of life," he said.
He added the government should consider "immediate financial support" to help the leisure industry through the next 12 months and ongoing investment into leisure centre stock.
If approved, the increases would also apply at St John's Sports Centre and Nunnery Wood Sports Complex, both of which are owned by Freedom Leisure.
Gym-goers at Perdiswell had mixed views on the price increases – with some saying they were not surprised.
Sue Guest said: "I've had two hip replacements so I come and do the aqua swim, it's very beneficial to me.
"It would be a shame if they increase it, but then they (the operators) have their own expenses as well.
"I think it's still reasonable value for money, actually."
Colin English, a pensioner, said: "I use the gym quite a lot, I come at least four or five times a week.
"They put the price up last year – if they do it again by these sorts of amounts I may have to reconsider because it's getting expensive."
Another gym user called Vinny added: "It feels like everything is going up in price at the moment.
"I'd never stop going though, this gym is important to me so I really don't mind."
A final decision is expected to be made on 24 November, subject to discussions at two city council committees before then.

headline: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
body:
Fishermen return to sea under a crimson sky in August after China's Jiangsu province is hit by Super Typhoon Dolphin
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.
A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.
In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.
Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts : hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.
It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.
In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.
This riverside park in the south-eastern Chinese city of Nanning was submerged by Tropical Storm Narra
August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties .
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.
The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.
El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.
The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.
Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El Niño predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.
China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El Niño.
Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.
China has seen back-to-back typhoons as the 2026 El Niño intensifies
In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.
To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people.
They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.
In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.
Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.
Tide of rubbish blankets Philippines river in August after weeks of monsoon rains
Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season , and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.
The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.
But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El Niño is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently.
"How severely a community experiences an El Niño is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock.
"Every El Niño tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

headline: Delhi air quality worsens ahead of Diwali as firework restrictions enter force
body:
Air pollution is an annual problem in Delhi and large parts of northern India
Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality to India's capital.
The city's air quality index (AQI) - which measures PM2.5, fine particulate matter that can clog lungs - has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category and raising health concerns for millions of residents.
Breathing such polluted air over prolonged periods can cause respiratory problems and worsen existing illnesses, with children and older people particularly vulnerable.
Authorities have responded by invoking Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), introducing measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other sources of pollution.
GRAP is a set of emergency measures that become progressively stricter as pollution levels rise. The latest restrictions include more intensive road cleaning, higher parking charges to discourage private vehicle use and increased public transport services. Delhi Metro has introduced 20 additional weekday train trips, while authorities have been directed to stagger government office timings to ease traffic congestion.
Officials said the measures were introduced after forecasts suggested air quality would remain very poor over the coming days.
Delhi and neighbouring parts of northern India grapple with hazardous air every winter, particularly around Diwali, one of India's biggest festivals, which is just days away.
The festival is celebrated with lights, lamps and fireworks, which often worsen the city's already poor air quality by releasing fine particles and harmful gases into the atmosphere.
The annual pollution crisis is driven by a combination of factors, including vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, falling temperatures, low wind speeds and the burning of crop stubble in neighbouring states.
The sharp rise in pollution follows an unusually clean October, when Delhi recorded its lowest average AQI for the month in eight years.
Experts have attributed the sudden deterioration to falling temperatures, slow winds and an increase in crop-residue burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab and Haryana.
A recent storm had brought rain and stronger winds, helping clear the air. But as the weather settled, northwesterly winds returned, carrying smoke from burning fields towards the capital.
India's pollution watchdog classifies AQI readings between 301 and 400 as "very poor", while anything above 400 is considered "severe". On Wednesday morning, Delhi's AQI stood at 377.
The index takes into account eight major pollutants, including PM2.5 - tiny particles about 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair that can penetrate deep into the lungs.
Firecrackers set off during Diwali release particulate matter and gases into the air, adding to the existing pollution
With Diwali just days away, there are concerns that fireworks could push pollution levels even higher.
Last year, Delhi woke up to a toxic haze the morning after the festival, despite a court directive to use less-polluting firecrackers.
Authorities have imposed restrictions on firecrackers over the years, including outright bans on their manufacture, sale and use, but enforcing them has proved difficult.
On Monday, India's Supreme Court allowed the manufacture, sale and use of certified green firecrackers in Delhi and neighbouring areas for a limited period.
It said the crackers could be set off only between 06:00 and 07:00 local time (00:30-01:30 GMT) and between 20:00 and 22:00 (14:30-16:30 GMT) on 7 and 8 November, during the Diwali weekend.
The court also banned fireworks within 300m of hospitals, care homes, schools and other designated silence zones.
Green firecrackers use modified chemical formulations designed to produce fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. They must carry QR codes that allow buyers and authorities to verify details of their manufacturer and certification.
But ensuring that only approved firecrackers are sold remains a major challenge.
In its latest order, the Supreme Court acknowledged that conventional firecrackers had continued to be sold as green alternatives, even when a complete ban was in place.
Even Mumbai, India's financial capital, has recorded very high levels of pollution in recent days
It has directed police to patrol designated sales areas, carry out random QR-code checks and seize illegal firecrackers.
During particularly severe pollution episodes, Delhi authorities have also introduced measures such as hybrid schooling, work-from-home arrangements and restrictions on certain vehicles.
The problem is not confined to the capital. Mumbai, India's financial hub, has also recorded elevated pollution levels over the past month, despite benefiting from coastal winds that typically help disperse pollutants.
On 24 October, Mumbai's AQI had reached 322, placing it in the "very poor" category. The spike was attributed to a combination of low wind speeds, construction dust, garbage burning, firecracker emissions and pollutants carried from neighbouring regions.
The city's air quality has improved in recent days - and it recorded an AQI of 89, classified as "satisfactory", on Wednesday. Neighbouring Navi Mumbai recorded a "moderate" AQI of 118.
The improvement follows nearly two weeks of smoggy conditions, with residents sharing photos and videos of the haze on social media.
