headline: Weapon or wine bottle? China disputes reports of artillery shell in Papua New Guinea
body:
The 32kg object was found at a construction site in Port Moresby
Chinese authorities have dismissed reports that a suspected China-made artillery shell was found in a commercial shipping container in Papua New Guinea, saying it is a "shell-shaped wine bottle".
"It poses no danger at all," the Chinese embassy wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday, drawing sceptical comments.
Police in Port Moresby arrested four Chinese nationals last Friday after the 32kg object was found at a construction site in the capital city.
Authorities were looking into whether it was a live device, local reports said then, with police commissioner David Manning describing it as "a very concerning discovery".
In a report on Wednesday, the Australia Broadcasting Corporation cited unnamed sources identifying the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 Artillery Projectile that contains chemical explosives and a fuse. The BBC has not independently verified this.
Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the object was "merely a dummy", local newspaper Post Courier said.
However, the Chinese embassy said in its statement that it is "virtually impossible" for an illegal military-grade artillery shell to be smuggled out of China to Papua New Guinea.
"China enforces some of the world's strictest firearm control laws and regulations," it wrote, adding that China is "widely recognised as one of the safest countries globally".
Some Facebook users appear unconvinced.
"What sort of wine bottle weighs 32 kilograms?" wrote one of them.
Another wrote that the object bore no labels indicating that it's a wine bottle.

headline: After the US midterms, what will a lame duck Trump mean for the global economy?
body:
Republicans’ crushing setback will play out in stock markets, inflation, interest rates and economic growth
Donald Trump’s loss of control of the House of Representatives and the Senate has put the world economy on notice for an unpredictable final two years of his presidential term.
After Democrats swept aside his Republican party in the midterm elections, analysts said the prospect of a highly erratic lame-duck president would have significant implications for financial markets, growth, inflation, government borrowing costs and living standards.
Here are the biggest expected consequences for the US economy and for other countries.
Markets initially dropped in early trading in Asia overnight but rallied as investors weighed up the midterm results.
Investors typically dislike uncertainty and political chaos. The fact that the president conceded the result and acknowledged the impact of the Iran war has been taken as a positive in markets. However, his warning that he will become “Mr Veto” raises the prospect of a turbulent finale to his time in the White House.
Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg, said the result showed that US voters had “rejected Trump and his somewhat authoritarian penchant for crony capitalism. [That] shows that US institutions and its checks and balances work. That is a positive, in my view.”
Much of the outlook for stock markets, inflation and growth is contingent on the war in the Middle East and the pace of the advance of artificial intelligence.
Traders expect the Democrats to take a tougher line on AI regulation and the datacentre rollout, raising questions over a driver of stock market growth. There are also concerns that Trump, with the midterms out of the way and his control over domestic policy weakened, could take a more aggressive approach to foreign policy, with the potential to intensify the war in Iran.
The cost to US households from surging inflation triggered by a deeply unpopular war, alongside a chaotic tariff policy that has devastated small businesses, was key to the midterm result. US diesel prices surged to a record high in August , while the headline inflation rate has risen to 3.7%.
The US-Israeli invasion of Iran, leading to the closure of the critical strait of Hormuz, reignited global inflationary pressures amid the biggest energy price shock of the modern age.
The oil price fell back on Wednesday, dropping by as much as 9% to trade below $100 a barrel for the first time in a month, as investors digested the midterm results amid hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough on Iran. Trading at about $94, Brent crude, the international benchmark, remains significantly higher than its prewar level of about $70. As a consequence, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) expects global headline inflation to rise to 4.7% this year, with energy-importing countries hardest hit.
The possibility of Trump ramping up hostilities against Iran would add to the inflationary shock, but it would also further add to his unpopularity.
Higher inflation has forced central banks to raise interest rates, with the US Federal Reserve defying pressure from Trump by increasing the cost of borrowing for the first time since 2023.
Against a volatile backdrop in the war and as inflationary pressures persist, investors anticipate at least one more rate increase from the Fed. The Bank of England is expected on Thursday to raise rates , while the European Central Bank is also expected to push up borrowing costs.
After losing control of Congress, the Republicans will lack the votes to confirm new appointments to critical public bodies, including new Fed governors. Trump could still use his veto powers, which can be overturned only if two-thirds of both chambers agree.
Higher inflation and interest rates triggered by the Iran war have driven up borrowing costs, adding to the pressure on countries with high levels of public debt.
In the US, the logjammed political system will face its first major test on 11 December, when politicians have to agree to authorise government spending to avoid a shutdown . The gridlock could prevent Trump from launching new tax and spending measures, which could cut two ways, restricting the capacity for fiscal stimulus to boost the economy, but also limiting a further rise in borrowing and debt.
Analysts say the crushing midterm defeats for Maga candidates will hurt the president’s authority and could pave the way for more cooperation between Republicans and Democrats in Congress.
Analysts say political turbulence and presidential actions on trade and immigration could put US growth at risk, but inflation and, most importantly, the prospects for de-escalation in the Middle East are the main factors to watch.
Investors are wary that a clampdown by the Democrats on AI could hit investment and growth in the US. The spillovers from the tech boom have been felt around the globe, with AI investment helping to bolster the UK economy.
However, tech industry leaders were already cooling on the rollout of AI amid concerns over cyber risks. Many investors also feared the emergence of a bubble in the US stock market. Analysts at Allianz say the scale of AI investment, and its capacity to power global economic growth, could mean the left-right political playbook is less predictable than in the past. Environmental and social impacts are also increasingly important considerations.
As recently as last month the IMF forecast that US growth would remain stable at 2.3% this year and next, despite the heightened risks to activity caused by the Iran war and the uncertain path for AI investment.
Analysts at Berenberg said US growth could slow to about 1.5% in 2028 amid political gridlock, a slowdown over AI and a drag from Trump’s crackdown on immigration. As a result, the US would contribute less to global growth than before, they said.

headline: The Guardian view on EU ‘Made in Europe’ rules: a fatal blow to Brexiter delusions | Editorial
body:
It is getting ever harder for Eurosceptics to deny that it was an economic and strategic blunder for Britain to leave the single market
T he EU is a constantly evolving institution. The rules keep changing and, since Britain is destined by geography to want a close economic relationship with the bloc, there will always be something to negotiate in Brussels.
Most of those discussions over the past two years have been uncontroversial, except in the eyes of dogmatic Eurosceptics. That doesn’t mean the talks have been easy. They never are with a club of 27 nations. But later this month, at a summit with the EU commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, Andy Burnham is expected to complete a treaty covering closer cooperation in a wide range of areas, including elimination of customs barriers to agricultural goods, a youth-mobility programme and integration with the EU’s carbon emissions trading scheme.
The agenda was set by Sir Keir Starmer as part of his intended “ reset ” of EU relations. Mr Burnham has since pledged to move further and faster towards closer ties, although he remains bound by his predecessor’s manifesto prohibition on membership of the single market and customs union this side of a general election.
What the prime minister can achieve in that space will be determined partly by his judgment of what domestic public opinion will allow, but more immediately by the terms of the European Commission’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act. This legislative package, more commonly called “ Made in Europe ”, mobilises public procurement rules to insulate continental industries from what many EU political leaders see as unfair overseas competition – chiefly from China. Industrial policy and protectionism on such a scale is a symptom of the way a once-globalised trading system has in recent years fractured into rivalry between continental blocs. China’s colossal trade surplus, causing panic among European car manufacturers, for example, is one side of that story. Donald Trump’s capricious tariff wars are another.
Britain looks perilously isolated in such a world, which is why Mr Burnham is keen to find some accommodation within the Made in Europe regime. That isn’t straightforward, given that the essential purpose of the new rules will be to benefit enterprises in the single market to the deliberate disadvantage of those on the outside, which includes Brexit Britain. Some compromise is available, with the UK recognised as a “trusted partner”, but that status won’t be accorded simply as a reward for pro-European vibes from Labour. Mr Burnham’s declarations of strategic intent are helpful, but there will be a lot of hard bargaining ahead on the terms of a deal. Without one, Britain’s carmaker and other industries would face crippling new trade barriers.
For that reason, the “Made in Europe” question has shot up the government’s agenda. The Eurosceptic opposition parties, meanwhile, are silent on the subject. To acknowledge the existence of a problem would mean recognising Britain’s disadvantaged status outside the single market, which is a refutation of the founding case for Brexit . Mr Burnham will not find it easy to negotiate the next stage of Britain’s reintegration with the EU, but those who resist his direction of travel will find it ever harder to pretend there is any alternative.

headline: The great sleeping giant of America has awakened | Robert Reich
body:
The real question in my mind is whether Democrats will take advantage of the new age of populism
The great sleeping giant of the US has awakened, taken a hard look at what’s become of the nation, and roared a thunderous “NO!”
What occurred on Tuesday was not – as some are saying – the inevitable midterm swing of the pendulum against the party in power. Texas hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1988. The last time Kansas elected a Democratic senator was 1932.
Nor was it just the economy . Americans are unhappy with high prices, to be sure, but inflation isn’t out of control. The country is not in a depression or recession. Unemployment remains quite low.
Nor, finally, was it all due to Donald Trump . Despite Trump’s repeated efforts to get voters to “pretend” he was on the ballot, he was not. Most Republican candidates barely mentioned him and many Democratic candidates stressed local or statewide issues rather than fixate on him.
Something much larger is responsible for what occurred: anti-establishment populism. It’s burst forth against the mammoth corporations that have scored record profits while most Americans have had to pay more. Against the mega donors and super Pacs that have flooded US politics with more campaign money – legalized bribes – than ever before.
And against the big tech billionaires who have become the most powerful force in the US economy and society – as well as Trump’s and the Republican party’s most visible backers.
The irony is that anti-establishment anger propelled Trump into the presidency in 2016 and again in 2024. Many Americans had found his politically incorrect rants and “America first” nativism to reflect their own anger at being disrespected and left behind. “I am your warrior,” he told supporters when he announced his candidacy for the 2024 election.
But during his second term, Trump has morphed into the very establishment he had railed against. He gave tax cuts and subsidies to tech billionaires. He’s promoted their AI, pushed their datacenters, put Elon Musk in charge of the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge), advocated their crypto, and went to war in the Middle East – not only causing gas prices to soar but making big oil billions (or, as Trump bafflingly boasts, “we’re making an absolute fortune in our country”) and enriching big tech weapons makers and investors, including his family.
Many who voted for Trump in 2016 and 2024 have now abandoned him because of this blatant corruption, crony capitalism and eagerness to be on the gilded side of the US’s new Gilded Age. According to CNBC’s late October poll, corruption was the top issue on voters’ minds.
Meanwhile, anti-establishment populism has taken firm hold in the Democratic party. “The biggest divide in this country is not left versus right,” said the newly elected Texas Senate candidate James Talarico. “It’s top versus bottom.”
Sherrod Brown regained his Senate seat from Ohio largely due to voter anger at datacenters and the big tech billionaires behind them.
Abdul El-Sayed never tired on the campaign trail of reminding Michigan voters that his opponent, Mike Rogers, was backed by big corporations and mega donors.
after newsletter promotion
Even Kansas’s victorious Adam Hamilton – who during his run for the Senate adamantly rejected the leftist label his opponent wanted to impose on him – campaigned on making datacenters pay for their own energy, banning lawmakers from trading stocks, expanding Medicare drug-price negotiations, and cracking down on price-gouging.
Hamilton also rejected money from corporate Pacs, as did most Democratic candidates for the Senate.
The real question in my mind is whether, come January when they control Congress, Democrats will take advantage of the new populism to enact measures most Americans need, such as Medicare for All, and reforms most Americans want, such as tougher anti-monopoly laws and limits on campaign contributions (even if this requires a constitutional amendment).
Trump is likely to veto any such initiatives, of course, but at least they’ll lay down markers for the 2028 presidential election – which, judging from what we’ve seen in the midterms, is likely to be a populist doozie.
Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com . His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

headline: UK government considers smart glasses ban over secret filming concerns
body:
Minister hints at restriction on selling technology ‘to certain users’ amid worries over surreptitious filming of women
The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said.
Speaking in the House of Commons , the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.
Kaur said: “The benefits of smart glasses must be weighed against the harms they can cause. The government is already looking into options to restrict smart glasses in certain settings and restricting the sale to certain users.”
The minister said people who used smart glasses for filming already risked breaking the law in certain settings, such as in a court where cameras are prohibited.
Kaur added: “Other settings, such as healthcare and education, have existing safeguarding or professional policies that are relevant to smart glasses and any kind of digital recording. NHS England and the Department for Education are currently looking into wearable technology in certain settings as well.”
Anna Sabine, a Liberal Democrat MP and a culture spokesperson for the party who held Wednesday’s debate, said: “Women are reporting waking up after nights out to find videos of themselves have gone viral online, filmed without their knowledge or consent by men wearing smart glasses.
“To me, these devices not only have the potential to erode safety and privacy in public spaces, but raise really important questions about consent.”
after newsletter promotion
She said one of the selling points of the glasses in advertisements was that they could be used “to film discreetly”. Sabine said she did not want parliamentarians to “only regulate once it is too late”.
Kaur said smart glasses, which can come with built-in cameras, microphones and displays, could “be hugely beneficial” to some people. “For example, for those that are visually impaired, smart glasses have been a gamechanger, helping them navigate the world around them.”
A politician in the Senedd has defended his use of smart glasses in the debating chamber. Jason O’Connell, a Reform UK MS for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr, read a speech from an in-built teleprompter feature in his glasses last month.
He told the BBC’s Politics Wales: “One of the things I identified, a weakness of mine, was that my head was down looking at my notes a lot and I wanted to get away from that.”

headline: LIV Golf’s attempted relaunch collapses after new lead investor withdraws, reports say
body:
BC Partners reportedly walks away after player exodus
LIV set to appear at bankruptcy hearing on Thursday
The rebel LIV Golf tour’s attempt to relaunch itself after filing for bankruptcy has collapsed following the withdrawal of the new lead investor BC Partners, according to reports on Wednesday.
The private capital firm made the decision to walk away after struggling to convince several star players to commit fully to the league going forward, the Financial Times and the Athletic reported, citing anonymous sources.
The once free-spending Saudi-backed league that turned the golf world upside-down by luring superstars away from the traditional PGA Tour is now expected to have its remaining assets liquidated.
The tour is expected to appear at a Thursday hearing in a bankruptcy court ‌in Trenton, New Jersey, to discuss various contracts, leases and assets. It is unclear whether LIV’s ultimate fate may also be discussed.
LIV Golf did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had poured an estimated $5bn into the tour since 2022, before abruptly pulling the plug earlier this year.
LIV formally filed for bankruptcy protection in September, though officials vowed to relaunch as “LIV 2.0” next season with a shorter schedule and reduced prize money, and equity stakes in the league for players. The new lead investor BC Partners Credit had pledged an initial funding commitment of a potential $300m.
However, several players including Spain’s Jon Rahm and Sergio García announced publicly their decisions to withdraw from the new version of the tour in recent weeks. Several others were believed to be on the fence. Bryson DeChambeau – arguably the breakaway circuit’s biggest name, who continued to back the tour – did not commit publicly to returning.
LIV’s attempt to relaunch was made more complicated after the DP World Tour reversed its policy of allowing golfers to appear in events on both tours, instead forcing player such as Rahm to choose.
The DP World Tour chief executive, Guy Kinnings, told the Scotsman on Tuesday that he had a duty “to protect the Tour against an entity who spent, so we are told, over $7bn, with one of their aims being to ‘destroy the DP World Tour’”.
Rory McIlroy, an outspoken critic of LIV, on Wednesday lent his support to Kinnings’s stance and said he also believed LIV had set out to eradicate its rivals. Speaking before the DP World Tour playoff Abu Dhabi Championship event, he said: “I agree with everything that Guy said. They took players; they took sponsors; they turned professional golf into an arms race. They were going around Augusta saying ​they wanted to destroy the European Tour .
“It’s ironic that a week later, now they are talking about ‘completing and not competing’ and all that. That’s different from what they were saying at the start of the year.
“It was always going to be good for a few years until something like this happened, or they realised they weren’t going to get any return on investment, or they were going to leave the golf space and go invest in something else ⁠and invest in something that would actually make them money,” McIlroy said.
McIlroy, who plays on the PGA Tour and ​DP World Tour, believes men’s golf needs a reset. “I ​think we’ll look back on it as a ​very strange time,” he said.
“It gave players a lot of leverage over the tours, and I don’t necessarily think that’s a ​good thing for the overall health ‌of the professional game. ​I think there has to be a ​balance there. There has to be a bit of give and take.
“You know, I’ve said this from the start, like there’s never been a better time to be a professional golfer. Talk to Jack Nicklaus or any of these older guys, they would have loved LIV to come around in their day. They would have made more money, and we are all making more money because of it. But I do think there has to be a bit of a ‌reset.”
Documents from bankruptcy filings showed that LIV owes between $500m and $1bn in estimated liabilities to at least 1,000 creditors, including star players.
Rahm, DeChambeau and Dustin Johnson hold the largest unsecured claims against the tour, totalling more than $5m each.

headline: ‘It’s just vape shops, nail shops, charity shops’: can anything save the British high street?
body:
It’s 20 years since Jo and Richard Hill bought anything in Rotherham town centre. Why have they and so many locals abandoned it for the nearest retail park – and what would it take to change their minds?
O n 22 May 1987, retail history was made in Rotherham. Parkgate Retail World, thought at the time to be the UK’s largest open-air shopping centre, welcomed shoppers for some one-stop retail therapy. The official opening was marked in swanky fashion with a “breathtaking” display from Marlboro’s red-and-white branded biplanes, followed by a “spectacular” laser show, the first in South Yorkshire. Helen Worth – Coronation Street’s Gail Platt – cut the ribbon before jovial local people jostled to fill their car boots with goods from Comet, Jolly Giant and Poundstretcher.
Almost 40 years on, the razzle is a bit less dazzling. Parkgate, as the retail park is called now, looks like any large big-box outdoor shopping centre you might find on urban fringes. There’s a Primark, a Sports Direct and a Matalan, plus (of course) a Frankie & Benny’s. Shoppers still seem to love it. “I think it’s ideal. It’s got everything here,” says Robert Gordon. The 66-year-old retired factory production manager had popped to Pets at Home to get a cupcake and toy for his dog Bruno’s fourth birthday.
Gordon has lived in Rotherham for 24 years. “A lot of people come to outlets like this. It’s very rare we go into the town centre and, if we did, we’d go to Sheffield,” he says. He is hardly an outlier. Almost half of Britons don’t visit their high street weekly. Instead, shoppers are opting for retail parks . Business is so strong, retailers are scrambling for spots, even paying extra to secure their place. By the end of 2025, only 4.8% of retail park lots in Britain were vacant, according to real estate consultancy Knight Frank – the lowest level on record. Vacancy rates for UK high streets, on the other hand, sit at 13% , reports Savills.
Gordon remembers a time two decades ago when you “couldn’t move” in Rotherham town centre, especially at the weekend. “It was packed and all the local shops were busy. Now these big outlets have taken over.” He admits his shopping habits come at a cost to the local community. “We are part of the problem,” he says. “It’s not progress. You used to meet people, but now you’re lucky to see anyone you know. Most people will come here and shop, get what they need and go back home.”
Jo Hill, 59, and her husband Richard, 65, are also Rotherham locals. Until recently, they hadn’t set foot in the town centre in nearly two decades. “What you see is either vape shops, nail shops or charity shops,” says Jo, who is semi-retired. Rotherham town centre is bookended by Parkgate at one end, and Meadowhall – one of the UK’s largest indoor shopping centres – at the other. The couple were visiting Parkgate to buy a printer from Currys. “For the big stuff, it’s either here or Meadowhall,” says Richard.
A short journey away, in Rotherham town centre, the picture is different. About 70 retail units, 24% overall, are vacant , far higher than the national average, and it is immediately apparent. One of the first things you see when leaving the train station is a derelict branch of BrightHouse, a rent-to-own retailer selling large appliances and furniture, which shut down in 2020. Further up is an anonymous-looking shopfront with smashed windows, graffiti and empty panelling where a shop sign should be – another shuttered chain, Fultons Foods, which closed in 2022. The only identifying mark is a window sticker: “There’s always change at Fultons.” Vape shops, discount chains and charity shops dominate the street.
The arrival of Parkgate Retail World nearly four decades ago wasn’t without friction. Even then, market traders expressed fears about the impact on business and, in Westminster, parliamentarians warned that these mini shopping metropolises would drain jobs from the high street, “ disembowel towns and villages ” and disadvantage those unable to drive .
Donna, who owns a furniture shop, and Saj, who runs a sandwich deli, are on their lunch break when I stop them. “It’s declined totally. I really wish it hasn’t, but it has,” says Donna. Nowadays she usually serves about four or five customers, and her daily takings have declined to “virtually nothing”, she says. Saj agrees that footfall is nonexistent.
The pair say safety is one reason that locals, especially elderly people, are staying home. “People have had their bags stolen, or been followed into banks; you’re watched when using the cash machines,” says Donna. “People will only come if they feel safe. It was always the older generation that came into the shop buying beds. Now their families won’t let them come out.” In 2023, a government analysis found that the number of crimes carried out per 1,000 people in Rotherham town was 160, 72% higher than the national average at the time. Recent police data shows there were 1,105 crimes, including 356 violent and sexual offences and 188 instances of shoplifting recorded in central Rotherham in August of this year alone. Nearby Sheffield city centre recorded 836 crimes in the same period. Donna says drug users also hang around her shopfront. “They sleep in my doorway sometimes. There’s needles and all sorts left. We’re not getting anybody into the shop because it looks bad.”
For Saj, the lack of affordable parking is another problem killing the high street. Car ownership has soared since the advent of the retail park. In 1971, 52% of households in Britain owned a car. A decade later, this had jumped to 60%, and by 2022 nearly three-quarters of households had a car. On its website, Parkgate touts its “over 2,000 free parking spaces”, all in one concentrated area.
Within Rotherham town centre, there are 1,610 spaces, which, until fairly recently, were all paid – though the council has recognised parking as a challenge. In 2016 it cut long-stay charges from £6.50 to £3.50 a day, and last year, it introduced free parking for one hour on weekdays. At the weekend, some spaces are free all day, but many, while acknowledging the council’s efforts, say it is not enough.
Sitting on a bench and lapping up the sun on Rotherham High Street are Leo Lopez and Claire Mercer. “I’ve seen a massive change,” says 50-year-old Lopez, a support worker. Mercer, also 50, a road safety campaigner, agrees. “You don’t come here to do general shopping after 3.30pm. It’s aggro caused by drugs mainly. People are more out of their head by that time. It’s an unfortunate truth, but it’s everywhere.”
The state of the town centre “deteriorates the morale”, says Lopez. And it may be contributing to the rise of rightwing populism: research by the thinktank Power to Change published last year found higher support for Reform UK in areas with run-down high streets that have high vacancy rates. Mercer says a part of town filled with ethnic minority shops and restaurants has been disparaged by some as “a foreign bazaar”. “Would they prefer the shops were empty? It’s much better to have busy shops, but people don’t like change.”
T he town centre isn’t totally devoid of good news. Days before I came to town, Yella Brick Road – a quirky clothing and homewares shop – was preparing to close its doors, a decision it reversed after loyal shoppers flocked to keep the business afloat. Owner Dannii Paston has been trading in the town centre for 17 years. “Recently, people are just careful with money. We’re a shop where you don’t need anything in here – it’s all treat spends,” she says.
Surprisingly, it was the relocation of Primark, the supposed big, bad clothing behemoth, that Paston believes cost her the most business. “I didn’t think they were our customers, but actually, people would go to Primark for certain things like pants, tights or a cheap dress for the 10-year-old, then come to us for themselves,” she says. Even when the chains were in the town centre, their limited stock couldn’t compete with their warehouse-sized counterparts in Parkgate, says Paston. “It’s a societal shift on how people want to shop. Why would you go into a tiny high-street shop that’s got a quarter of the selection?
She believes supermarkets were the first to pull customers from town. In many large Morrisons branches, for example, you can take your passport photo, wash your clothes in an on-site launderette and even have keys cut while doing the weekly shop. Sainsbury’s has closed 420 Argos high-street shops since 2020, after acquiring its parent company, and shifted them inside its larger stores. “It’s like a little high street,” says Paston.
The out-of-town shopping destination – whether it’s a retail park, mall or outlet – hasn’t always been part of British life. The UK’s first such complex, Gem Superstore, opened in West Bridgford, Nottingham in 1964. Operated by an American company, Government Employees Mart, it brought US-style shopping to Britain – and demand was through the roof. The Goldfinger star Shirley Eaton was brought in for the official opening day, when 30,000 people rushed down its aisles. At 110,000 sq ft, fairly paltry compared with the sprawling shopping complexes that followed, it was more akin to a modern-day large supermarket. Two years later, Asda, then still a fledgling chain of small grocers, bought the site for its first superstore.
London’s Brent Cross Shopping Centre, which opened in 1976, took things to the next level. Traders feared that the 800,000 sq ft behemoth – boasting air conditioning (unheard of at the time) and the triple threat of Fenwick, John Lewis and Marks & Spencer under the same roof – would hammer local trade, and the Labour government tried to thwart the development. But Barnet council, in a Tory stronghold where Margaret Thatcher held her parliamentary seat, gave it the enthusiastic thumbs up. The indoor shopping centre opened the year after Thatcher’s ascendancy to leader of the opposition in 1975. Already there was consensus among local authorities that out-of-town shopping centres would destroy high streets but, after the Tories entered Downing Street in 1979, planning rules were eased. “There is a change of attitude in the 1980s which begins to allow these out-of-town locations,” says Alistair Kefford, the chair of urban studies at Leiden University in the Netherlands. In 1981, there was one out-of-town retail park in the UK . By 1988, there were 90 and at the end of 1996, there were 385.
In the end, the critics were right. “There’s only a certain level of consumer demand within a regional economy,” says Kefford. “If you build a wonderful, shiny, exciting new shopping mall or retail park, it doesn’t create a lot of new shoppers. They just stop going somewhere else.”
The bruising figures bear this out. In 2024, 13,479 shops across the UK closed their doors . While retail accounts for 5% of the UK economy and less than a tenth of employment, an area’s former glory is often starkly highlighted by its decrepit high street. “Dying high streets make people feel ashamed of their place, that their life is falling apart,” says Eddie Blake, a director at the architecture practice Studio Weave.
How to save the high street has become fertile political territory. Parkgate lies within John Healey’s constituency. In 2019, the now-chancellor scolded M&S for shutting its branch in the shopping complex, about a decade after relocating from Rotherham town centre, meaning the retailer would “disappear from the town for the first time in 125 years”. Since entering No 11, Healey has said “blighted” high streets will soon be “on the up”. Last month, Andy Burnham announced £210m in funding to regenerate down-on-their-luck high streets. But Kefford is sceptical. “Retail is a barometer – it’s not an engine. Where you see retail doing well, it’s a sign that the regional economy itself is doing well, but retail by itself won’t make a place wealthy. It’s not an engine of growth because it relies on people spending their disposable income,” he says.
Efforts to turn the ship can often be futile. “Once a location has set off down a particular path, it’s very hard to get out of it. In fact, everything leads further and further down that path. The narrowing range of shops, the growth of empty properties – these are things that snowball and get worse and worse,” says Kefford.
So, are UK high streets doomed? Shops “are probably not going to come back”, says Kefford, but there’s still hope. “In the 1950s and 1960s, town centres sustained loads of uses. There were many more houses and social activities: churches, working men’s clubs, community associations, charities, theatres. We need to think more fundamentally and creatively about what is the point of a town centre,” he says.
This may be good for society, too. Blake says the retail parks and shopping centres, and the cars we use to get to them, contribute to an “atomised culture that makes people feel alone”. A multifunction high street can better facilitate social interaction: “The small-grain interactions of social life are better, higher quality, and more frequent.”
Until then, many of us will be drawn to these bland, uninspiring shopping pens on the fringes of town. On my way to the train station, the No 8 bus pulls up on the high street, having just stopped at Parkgate. Sure enough, the passengers who alight are carrying bags from Primark, TK Maxx and Sports Direct.

headline: Once it was a £1 hanger. Now it’s a £15 locker. Why do cloakrooms cost so much on a night out?
body:
The cost of checking your coat or bag is galloping ahead of other – also rising – prices at venues. We explain the surprisingly complex reasons why
Not long ago, it cost just £2 to put a coat or a heavily stuffed tote bag in a cloakroom on a night out. But over the course of the 2020s, that cost has increased to more than £13 in some UK venues.
At the Outernet Live venue complex in London’s Soho, it costs £11 to put a bag in a large locker. It’s £9 at east London nightclub Fold, and at north London’s Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, they cost up to £13.20 . At the Warehouse Project in Manchester, large bags must be stored at a nearby Premier Inn at £11.99 per locker. Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena has a dedicated bag storage facility which costs £15 for large bags. It’s £9.99 near the 3,000-capacity Edinburgh Playhouse and £9.90 at Testbed in Leeds. How have double-digit cloakroom costs like these been normalised?
The price rises are helping to push average spending per head on a night out from £20.95 in 2020 to £28.06 in 2026, according to Night Time Industries Association. “For years, nightlife businesses have faced relentless increases in the cost of operating, from energy and employment to taxation, business rates and supply chains,” says chief executive Michael Kill. “Many have had no choice but to pass some of those costs on to consumers simply to keep their doors open. But the reality is that consumers have now hit an affordability ceiling.”
With consumers spending less on alcohol, locker systems and cloakrooms offer premises a way to make some of that money back, but, Kill says, “the consumer cannot be the industry’s financial shock absorber indefinitely”.
UK storage policy changed after the 2017 attack at an Ariana Grande concert in Manchester Arena which killed 22 people and injured more than 1,000. “Martyn’s law” legislation requires “appropriate public protection measures” at public events to reduce the risk and impact of terror attacks. It led to many venues – including the nationwide network of 18 Academy Music Group sites – banning bags over A4 size entirely and offloading them to external lockers or storage partners. In London, these are often kebab shops, restaurants and barbers.
Carrie Wang, a London-based spin instructor, was buzzing to see Hot Chip at O2 Academy Brixton until she learned her near-empty tote bag had to be stored in a kebab shop round the corner. “I was fuming,” Wang says. “They charged me £10 and it wasn’t a proper facility, it was just a random storage room – it’s not like they had lockers and my things were actually safe there.” Academy Music Group did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Ahmed Khan is the owner of Kentish Delight, a kebab shop in Kentish Town. He says that in 2022, O2 Kentish Town Forum’s management asked if he had any spare space in the takeaway. “They had a look and said my premises are perfect and secure for the customer – and I said yes, why not?” Khan charges £5 per bag and says nothing has ever gone missing. “Although the bag people never buy kebabs.”
The high costs and added logistics mean that some people are taking risks with their belongings. At an AEW wrestling event at Wembley Arena, fans were directed to a nearby Premier Inn to stow their bags, at £10 a pop with long queues.
Soul singer Danny Toeman decided to stuff his rucksack behind a carpark vending machine. “I could stuff most of the valuable contents into my pockets,” says Toeman. “So I thought: let’s just stash it somewhere and if it gets stolen, so what?”
That in itself is a security risk – if staff had seen Toeman’s backpack, the venue could have been evacuated. But it’s become commonplace. One Reddit user opted to hide their bag outside the O2 Academy in Southampton. “They will literally not let you in,” they wrote. “I was forced to leave it outside the building entirely and it was stolen when I came out.”
Willem Pelle is head of sales at eLockers, a Dutch company working with many UK nightclubs including Drumsheds, Fold and Warehouse Project. “When we expanded into the UK, we saw that many venues were facing staffing challenges following Covid, making traditional cloakrooms increasingly difficult to operate,” Pelle says.
London is their main UK market, with Manchester a close second. Pelle says there is typically no upfront cost for the venue, which gets to share the takings with eLockers, adding: “It’s important that the pricing works for both the venue and its customers, while creating a sustainable additional revenue stream.”
Some clubbers have reported benefits to lockers, such as those at Drumsheds, where you can put stuff in and out – allowing for outfit changes during an event. But not all venues opt to install expensive locker systems. At Hackney Bath House, the cloakroom is free. Sneaky Pete’s in Edinburgh installed lockers in 2012 and still charge £2 per locker. Peckham’s 200-capacity club the Carpet Shop charges £3 per item: “No need to charge more, it’s a tiny bit of space and a rail,” says general manager Cam Prentis.
He sees the cloakroom as a valuable part of the club experience in its own right. Upstairs and away from the bustle, it’s where staff and punters can have a break and a chat. “Whoever’s on the cloakroom has their own music playing,” Cam says. Unlike at an unstaffed array of lockers or the back room of a kebab shop, “it’s a vibe up there”.
Some names have been changed

headline: Why pharma firms are going to Earth’s orbit in search of new cancer drugs
body:
A space capsule 300 miles above us is growing the tiny crystals of a potential cancer drug in microgravity
R oughly 300 miles above our heads, three washing machine-sized capsules are orbiting the Earth. Inside one of them, tiny crystals of a potential cancer drug are being grown in the weightlessness of space. The others are testing heat protection materials and navigation systems for when the capsules plunge back through Earth’s atmosphere at hypersonic speeds. Together, they represent a small but significant step towards what some hope will become a lucrative new industry: manufacturing drugs and other materials in space.
The spacecraft belong to California-based Varda Space Industries. On 1 October, it launched two onboard the same rocket, followed by the third on 20 October. With a record three spacecraft now simultaneously in orbit for the first time, the company is edging closer to its ambition of operating a fleet of orbiting pharmaceutical factories.
“We’re the first company in human history to launch multiple commercial re-entry vehicles simultaneously, and as the frequency of launches increases, the once ‘crazy future’ of manufacturing products in space is becoming more and more certain,” said Will Bruey, Varda’s chief executive.
There are several reasons for wanting to manufacture certain materials in space, one of the most important being microgravity. On Earth, gravity causes particles suspended in liquids to settle, while differences in density create currents. Both can interfere with the growth of crystals. “If you are able to remove those effects, you can make crystals grow in a much more ordered sort of way,” said Dr Meganne Christian, mission manager for in-space manufacturing at the UK-based Satellite Applications Catapult.
For pharmaceutical companies, this could open up new ways of formulating medicines, as the size, shape and arrangement of drug crystals can affect how easily drugs dissolve, how stable they are and how they can be administered. In some cases, this could enable drugs that currently require intravenous infusions to be reformulated into more convenient injections.
Other materials, such as the semiconductors used in everything from smartphones to electric vehicles, could also benefit from being manufactured in space, where microgravity and the absence of air could help produce purer crystals with fewer defects.
“Personally, I would really love to try and make graphene in microgravity,” said Christian. “Theoretically, it is this incredible material, but in practice you get a whole lot of defects in the crystals. It’s a similar story for semiconductors. If you can reduce the number of defects, you can get a much higher-performing material.”
Scientists have been experimenting with manufacturing in microgravity for decades, particularly aboard the International Space Station (ISS). But the ISS has predominantly served as a “test kitchen” for scientific ideas and is scheduled to be retired around 2030. “It wasn’t necessarily designed with manufacturing in mind,” said Dr Ryan Reeves, deputy chief scientist for the ISS National Laboratory.
Several companies are developing commercial space stations to replace the ISS, while others are designing specialist laboratories and equipment for conducting experiments aboard them. Among them is the UK-based BioOrbit, which recently sent a microwave-sized laboratory to the ISS as a step towards the production of self-injected cancer drugs.
However, for large-scale manufacturing and certain industrial processes, “you need to get humans out of the picture, because we’re dirty, we cause vibrations, and we require a whole higher level of safety,” said Christian.
This is where Varda’s autonomous factories come in. Known as free-flyers, they hitch a ride into orbit aboard SpaceX rockets, carrying miniature laboratories in which materials can be processed without astronauts. Once the experiments are complete, a capsule separates from the spacecraft, plunges through the atmosphere and parachutes safely back to an uninhabited region of Earth.
Varda is among the furthest advanced in demonstrating this approach, having already returned several capsules from orbit. It plans to launch another seven missions in 2027, and a further 10 in 2028.
The ability to conduct experiments frequently is particularly important for drug development. “If scientists have to wait 10 years between experiments or even a year, that really doesn’t fit into the speed of modern drug development,” said Michael Reilly, Varda’s chief strategy officer.
While Varda’s manufacturing ambitions are focused on pharmaceuticals, other companies are developing similar systems to produce different materials. For example, Cardiff-based Space Forge is exploring a hybrid approach, in which semiconductor crystals grown aboard spacecraft could be returned to Earth and used as templates for growing larger quantities, much like a sourdough starter.
Its first spacecraft, ForgeStar-1, recently demonstrated some of the processes needed to manufacture these semiconductor “seed wafers”, although it has yet to produce a finished material and return it to Earth. Andrew Bacon, the company’s co-founder and chief technology officer, said they hope to demonstrate the entire manufacturing and return process before 2030.
For Bacon, recent developments, including Varda’s launches, suggest that space manufacturing is approaching a turning point. “Since we started in 2018, nobody was talking about it. Now a lot of companies [are] talking about it,” he said. “People are starting to take this market very seriously. It does feel like we’re at the start of a new Industrial Revolution.”
Falling launch costs and increasingly frequent commercial rocket flights have helped to fuel this optimism. But significant challenges remain, including demonstrating that the benefits of manufacturing in orbit justify the expense. “It’s not going to be commercially viable for every application,” said Christian. “We have to identify those high-value use cases where it makes sense to do the work in microgravity.”
Regulators will also need to adapt to accommodate space-manufactured products. Later this year, the UK’s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) is expected to publish a plan clarifying how existing medicines regulations will apply to drugs manufactured in orbit.
But for now, one of the biggest challenges is demonstrating that space manufacturing can deliver consistently reliable results. “To get something to a commercially viable point, it needs to be done again and again and again,” said Christian. “That’s what these capsules need to do. They need to demonstrate this repeat performance.”

headline: Kim Jong-un, crypto bros and a $6.3bn heist – podcast
body:
North Korea is said to be behind the theft from the crypto exchange Binance. How did they pull it off and what will they do with the money? Kalyeena Makortoff and Jean H Lee report
It was 8pm last Thursday when the panic alarms went off across the crypto world. Binance , the world’s biggest crypto exchange, had been hacked. The cryptocurrency revolution promised to take power from the fusty old central banks and put it in the hands of the people. But the hack exposed just how vulnerable crypto can be.
The Guardian’s banking correspondent, Kayleena Makortoff , tells Helen Pidd how Binance was hacked and how the news has shaken the crypto world. Almost immediately, the finger of blame was pointed squarely in one direction: North Korea . The journalist Jean H Lee explains why one of the poorest and most isolated countries in the world is believed to have pulled off the audacious heist, and what it might do with the money.
Archive sources: CBC News, CNN, YouTube

headline: Our house purchase is at risk from a frozen Revolut account
body:
Access to our £37,000 deposit in a savings account is restricted after a ‘routine security review’
My wife’s Revolut account was frozen in what it calls a “routine security review” over a week ago. Nothing has been requested from her – no documents, the source of funds, or ID – yet, as a result, our house deposit of £37,000 in a joint savings account is also restricted.
We’re approaching the completion of our property purchase and have given notice on our rental home. Direct debits are bouncing and we’re concerned about our credit records.
At one point Revolut also restricted my personal account, so we effectively had no access to any money. We keep being given deadlines for the restrictions to be lifted which are missed, and call centre staff, when we can get through, have little ability to find out what’s happening, or make anything happen. XWF , Oxfordshire
Banks have legal powers, under anti-money-laundering regulations, to freeze accounts if a sudden windfall, overseas payment or unusual activity raises concerns. They are not required to warn customers or explain if they suspect foul play, although customers can complain to the Financial Ombudsman Service if they believe a bank acted unfairly.
There’s no suggestion foul play was suspected in your wife’s case and things progressed swiftly after I got involved. Accounts were reinstated, nearly three weeks after being suspended, and your wife was offered £175 as a goodwill gesture. Revolut says regulatory constraints prevented it explaining. “We’re sorry our review process took longer than usual, and our communication didn’t reach its usual standards, particularly given the inconvenience during an important life moment,” it says.
We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us at consumer.champions@theguardian.com or write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject to our terms and conditions .

headline: Democrats take Congress in a blue wave. Here's what it means for your money
body:
With Democrats flipping control of Congress in the midterm election , the shift in power on Capitol Hill could reshape household budgets — from student loan bills and health insurance premiums to housing costs and taxes.
Experts say results show that rising costs were top of mind for voters.
"I see this election as a repudiation of the anti-affordability agenda from the Trump administration," said Daniel Bunn, president and CEO of the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan, nonprofit research organization.
"Whether that's the conflict in the Middle East or the tariffs, just top to bottom, it's clear to me that was a real concern of the electorate," he said.
White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in an emailed statement that the Trump administration has delivered "tangible wins to make life more affordable for American families." Officials "will continue to put hardworking American's first with or without support from Democrats," he wrote.
Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and Senate, which could make it easier for the party to advance legislation. They can also use hearings and investigations to press federal agencies and companies to answer for policies and practices that impact consumers, and exert leverage over confirmation of President Donald Trump's nominees.
But turning campaign promises into changes people feel in their finances won't be easy. Trump can veto bills a Democrat-controlled Congress passes, limiting how much of their agenda could become law. Based on projections, Democrats will lack the numbers needed to override a presidential veto.
Any changes will also take time: Newly elected members of Congress won't take office until January.
Here are eight ways Democrats’ new congressional majority could affect your money.
"Not surprisingly, the Dems are going to be keyed in on affordability with respect to healthcare," said Zach Gaumer, vice president of health policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a nonpartisan think tank.
Likely target areas include:
OBBBA made Trump's 2017 tax cuts permanent and added temporary tax breaks. These included new deductions for tip income , overtime earnings , seniors and auto loan interest , which will expire after 2028 without an extension.
Democrats may support extending these provisions. But as the Democrat-controlled Congress maps out its agenda, lawmakers will have to address the federal budget deficit. For fiscal year 2026, the budget deficit ballooned to nearly $2 trillion , the Treasury announced in October.
Newly elected Democratic senators James Talarico of Texas, Troy Jackson of Maine and Annie Andrews of South Carolina all campaigned on expanding the child tax credit . Earlier this year, Senate Democrats also floated ideas to expand the standard deduction and create income tax exemptions for lower-earning Americans — which are costly proposals, according to Bunn from the Tax Foundation.
"I've called these termites in the tax code," he said. "You cannot consistently narrow your base, especially for the income tax, and expect your spending priorities to be well-funded."
With Democrats in control of Congress, they are likely to hold hearings and subpoena Trump officials over the administration's student loan policies, said higher education expert Mark Kantrowitz.
One priority may be pressing the Education Department to fix the popular Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, which cancels the remaining federal student debt of eligible government and nonprofit workers after a decade. Over the summer, Trump officials reassessed repayment timelines, delaying some borrowers' forgiveness date by years.
Broad student loan forgiveness is unlikely: Trump could veto such a bill, and the Supreme Court blocked the Biden administration's plan. More attainable changes could include restoring tax-free treatment of forgiven student debt, raising the new borrowing caps and expanding repayment options — measures that may attract bipartisan support, Kantrowitz said.
Trump has also said he may support legislation capping federal student loan interest rates , a proposal that could give Democrats common ground in their push to ease borrowers’ costs.
Housing affordability was a key election issue, and Democrats will likely explore ways to deliver relief, such as introducing measures to help first-time homebuyers, according to an Oct. 30 analysis by Desjardins, a Canadian financial services company.
However, lawmakers generally have little direct impact on home prices, which are based on market conditions. Mortgage rates, too, are influenced by forces generally beyond congressional control. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which remains higher than it was before the Iran war — due at least partly to concerns about inflation eroding the value of those bonds — influences mortgage rates.
"Jumpstarting the housing market relies on a calmer geopolitical environment and bond market in the short run," plus more housing supply and a "more dynamic labor market in the long run," said Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com.
The bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act , which automatically became law July 11 without the president's signature due to a constitutional provision, is "a model for what can pass in a divided Washington," Krimmel said. It includes measures to encourage housing construction, reduce regulatory barriers, expand financing options and limit purchases of single-family homes by large institutional investors.
The incoming class of senators will have to address Social Security insolvency .
The program's trustees project that the trust fund Social Security relies on to help pay retirement benefits, formally known as the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, may be depleted in the fourth quarter of 2032. Without action from Congress before then, benefits could face an across-the-board cut of 22%.
A number of Democratic lawmakers and some Republicans have called for increased payroll taxes on high earners to help shore up Social Security.
A potential SECURE 3.0 bill — a follow-up to bipartisan retirement-savings laws passed in 2019 and 2022 — could help expand workers' access to workplace retirement plans like 401(k)s, for example, among a roster of other reforms, experts said.
"Trump promised to cap credit card rates at 10%," said Aaron Klein, a senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution, a think tank. "A Democratic Congress might be willing to do that."
Any such cap is likely to be closer to 36% than to the 10% cap Trump has sought, Jaret Seiberg, a financial services policy analyst at TD Cowen, an investment bank, wrote in a research note Wednesday. Lawmakers in the current Congress have proposed legislation with these thresholds.
A cap would likely be welcome news for low- and middle-income Americans, Klein said. They are more likely than wealthy households to use debt to finance their lives and to carry a credit card balance — and therefore owe interest on their charges, he said.
Cardholders might see other impacts of such a policy, such as lower credit limits and a clawback of certain card rewards, he said.
Democrats' takeover of Congress could stall efforts to put crypto-friendly regulations into federal law, but everyday investors shouldn't expect much to change immediately.
"Platforms will keep offering the products they offer today, and they still have friendly regulators at the SEC and CFTC who are approving an ever-wider range of crypto products," said Lee Reiners, a cryptocurrency regulation expert and lecturing fellow of economics at Duke University.
The election results could threaten the Clarity Act , which would give the Commodity Futures Trading Commission greater authority over cryptocurrency trading while reducing the Securities and Exchange Commission's role. The bill passed the House in July 2025 by a 294-134 vote, but failed to advance in the Senate in September on a 49-50 procedural vote . "CLARITY is dead," said Reiners, adding that he sees little chance of the bill passing during the lame-duck session before Democrats take control in January.
Any future legislation aimed at creating a regulatory framework for digital assets would likely need to address Democrats' concerns about investor protections and conflicts of interest involving Trump's crypto businesses, said Martin Mulyadi, an accounting professor at Shenandoah University.
The SEC and CFTC can also continue developing crypto-friendly rules without Congress. But those rules are easier for a future administration to reverse than legislation, said Marcel Miu, a certified financial planner and founder of Simplify Wealth Planning based in Austin, Texas. "I'd tell investors to size their crypto investments as if the rules could change repeatedly over the coming years," Miu said.
The Iran war has led oil prices — and those of gasoline, jet fuel, heating oil, diesel and other fuels refined from oil — to surge. That has trickled into higher prices across the U.S. economy, experts said.
Oil prices fell on Wednesday on hopes that the election outcome will push Trump to make a deal to end the war .
"Ending the war in Iran would be the biggest policy lever to reducing inflation," the Brookings Institution's Klein said.
A Democrat-led Congress could try to limit Trump's ability to continue the war, perhaps by cutting funding.
"Congress' biggest power is the power of the purse," Klein said. "Wars are expensive."
— CNBC's Lorie Konish and Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting.

headline: CVS Health plans to split itself up. Here's why a breakup could make sense now
body:
In this article
CVS Health plans to break itself up — and this time, the bet looks a lot more viable.
The healthcare conglomerate on Wednesday announced plans to split into two publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. CVS would separate its pharmacy business – including roughly 9,000 retail locations – from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark.
The move comes more than two years after CVS considered a breakup but ultimately walked away from the idea. At the time, analysts questioned whether the retail pharmacy business could survive on its own.
“Back then, the idea of retail standing alone was unthinkable,” Brian Tanquilut, senior equity research analyst at Jefferies, told CNBC.
But the economics of the businesses have changed: CVS's retail pharmacy business has become more consistently profitable, while its insurer, Aetna, has improved its performance despite persistently high medical costs in Medicare Advantage plans. That could make it easier for the company to separate the units — and for investors to recognize the value of each on its own, rather than valuing them together as one sprawling healthcare conglomerate.
“For us, it's showing the stability of the pharmacy,” Michael Cherny, senior research analyst at Leerink Partners, said in an interview. “This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome.”
CVS CEO David Joyner told CNBC’s "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday that back in 2024, the company was "in a turnaround" without the flexibility, cash or business performance to execute a split. Now, CVS has posted eight consecutive quarters of beating Wall Street earnings estimates and has raised its guidance several times over the last two years, thanks to improvement across its PBM, pharmacy and insurer.
Since taking the helm in 2024, Joyner has pursued an aggressive turnaround plan that involves $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs.
The company also now expects to generate at least $15.5 billion in operating cash flow in 2026, a roughly 70% increase from $9.1 billion in 2024, and says it has reached its leverage target ahead of schedule.
"What's changed in two years is the fact that we now can look at this business and the assets that are assembled and really determine, without any distress or without anything that we have to do, what is the right strategic decision to make," Joyner told analysts on a call Wednesday, adding that the decision comes "out of strength."
While investors have largely cheered CVS's progress in recent years, Wall Street appeared more pessimistic about Wednesday's announcement, as the company's shares dropped about 12%.
CVS's retail business has benefited from changes in the competitive landscape, including the widespread retrenchment and store closures of Walgreens, Rite Aid and other pharmacy operators over the last few years. That’s created opportunities for CVS to gain market share, some analysts told CNBC.
CVS has also introduced changes to its pharmacy reimbursement model. Its CostVantage program is designed to replace the traditional process with a more transparent, cost-based model. Some analysts say that has helped the company better align reimbursement with the cost of dispensing prescriptions and contributed to steadier profits.
Those developments represent a meaningful shift for a business that has faced years of pressure from declining prescription reimbursement, store closures and competition from online pharmacies and other retailers.
That doesn't mean the retail pharmacy has become a high-growth business. CVS's retail pharmacy segment remains a relatively low-margin operation, with adjusted operating margins of roughly 4% to 5%. But analysts say it may now be stable and profitable enough to operate independently – even if investors value it at a discount to CVS's other businesses.
In a note Wednesday, RBC Capital Markets analyst Ben Hendrix said the lower valuation investors assign to the retail pharmacy unit has weighed on CVS's overall value and obscured the earnings strength of businesses like Aetna and Caremark.
The underlying growth of the insurance and PBM businesses is also stronger than that of retail pharmacy, Tanquilut said, after accounting for changes to Caremark's rebate arrangements.
Aetna in particular has gotten a better handle on medical costs by exiting unprofitable markets, expanding value-based care models, and tightening utilization management.
The breakup also comes as Caremark faces mounting scrutiny over PBM practices, including state-level legal and regulatory challenges involving the businesses and their relationships with pharmacies.
Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban any one company from owning both a pharmacy and a PBM — thought the Arkansas measure has been held up in court. Cherny noted that legal hurdles involving PBMs in other states have continued to pile up.
“Through what seems to be a never-ending litany of state lawsuits, it feels like it's been under more pressure,” Cherny said. “It's unclear if it just became, for lack of a better term, too tenuous to move forward with those two entities combined as one. I’m not sure.”
Even so, Joyner told the Wall Street Journal that the company wasn’t splitting up because of regulatory issues. CVS has said the separation follows a strategic review and is intended to give each business greater focus and flexibility.
The move also marks a significant departure from the integrated healthcare strategy CVS spent years building.
CVS spent roughly $70 billion to acquire Aetna in 2018 and argued that combining health insurance, pharmacy benefit management, retail pharmacies and health providers under one roof would help coordinate care and create a competitive advantage. CVS was still promoting that model as recently as its investor day last year.
The proposed split suggests the company now sees more value in separating at least some of those businesses – though it is not abandoning vertical integration altogether.
Aetna and Caremark will remain together in the healthcare company, alongside CVS’s specialty pharmacy, its primary care clinic Oak Street Health and its home-visit provider Signify Health. The separate pharmacy company will include roughly 9,000 retail stores, mail pharmacy operations and MinuteClinic, a retail medical clinic located inside certain CVS locations.
Both sides are large enough that they can stand on their own, Cherny said. Caremark is one of the country's three largest PBMs, while CVS has one of the largest retail pharmacy footprints in the U.S.
But separating the company raises questions about how much of the commercial relationship between the businesses can survive.
The relationship has historically benefited both sides. As it stands, Caremark can use CVS's extensive retail footprint to offer members convenient access to prescriptions and steer them toward CVS locations through preferred pharmacy arrangements. Programs such as Maintenance Choice, for example, give eligible members the option to fill certain maintenance medications at CVS retail pharmacies or through mail order.
Those arrangements also helped direct prescription volume to CVS's stores, giving the retail pharmacy unit an important source of customers. Because the businesses shared a parent company, the financial benefits of that relationship ultimately went to CVS as a whole.
In a note, RBC's Hendrix also raised questions about how the split could impact Aetna's Medicare Advantage quality ratings, which determine whether health plans qualify for bonus payments from the government. Retail pharmacists have played a role in engaging Aetna members, and a separation could complicate that relationship.
But Joyner told analysts Wednesday that the synergy between the two businesses would be "preserved in commercial agreements between the two organizations," adding that "we don't need the integration of an operating structure."
Joyner said CVS will be working on those potential agreements over the next 15 to 18 months.
Preferred pharmacy networks are common across the industry, and separate ownership does not prevent Caremark from continuing to favor CVS pharmacies through negotiated arrangements, Cherny said. The difference is that under separate ownership, the profits from those arrangements would no longer accrue to a single company, he noted.
“The issue is not whether the companies can continue working together in some capacity, but whether any future contractual arrangements preserve the SAME competitive advantages and flexibility as today under common ownership,” Cherny said in an afternoon note on Wednesday.
Still, both businesses face challenges on their own.
Tanquilut cautioned that some of CVS's recent retail pharmacy gains have come as Walgreens and other competitors have closed stores, raising questions about whether the growth can be sustained. The business also remains exposed to consumer pressure and competition from online pharmacies.
Caremark, meanwhile, faces continued regulatory scrutiny and potential headwinds from changes to the federal 340B drug discount program, which requires drugmakers to offer discounted medications to eligible hospitals and other healthcare providers serving low-income and vulnerable patients.
CVS participates in the program by providing pharmacy services to those organizations, but tweaks to manufacturer data-sharing policies and potential reimbursement changes could weigh on that business in 2027, Tanquilut said.
Aetna, meanwhile, is still working through a multiyear plan to rebuild its margins, as it looks to improve the profitability of its Medicare Advantage business.
Ultimately, CVS is betting that the value of letting investors assess its businesses separately will outweigh the benefits of keeping them under one roof. The split will test whether each can thrive independently.

headline: Figma sinks after earnings beat as company prioritizes long-term growth with AI changes
body:
In this article
Figma shares tumbled 7% in extended trading after the company reported third-quarter results and guidance that surpassed Wall Street's predictions.
Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:
Figma's revenue grew about 43% year over year in the quarter, according to a statement . Net loss narrowed to $81.3 million, or 15 cents per share, compared with a loss of $1.10 billion, or $2.72 per share, a year earlier.
The company's 12% adjusted operating margin exceeded the 6.1% consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount.
Executives lifted the full-year forecast. Figma now anticipates an 11% operating margin, up from 9% as of August, and $1.497 billion to $1.499 billion in revenue, compared with $1.463 billion to $1.467 billion before. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $1.471 billion in 2026 revenue.
The company sees fourth-quarter revenue growth slowing to about 33%. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted 28% growth.
Figma's announcement comes a day after highly valued design software startup Canva said it would cut 22% of its employees.
Shares have come down about 41% so far in 2026, while the S&P 500 index has gained 12%. Earlier this year, investors became concerned that artificial intelligence models could pose a competitive risk to Figma. Across much of software, AI panic has largely subsided as incumbents have posted persistent growth.
Figma wants to benefit from the rising adoption of AI to build websites and apps. During the quarter, the company started giving more AI credits to clients while maintaining prices.
"What that means is you're potentially trading off near-term revenue, investing in your customers, and then allowing yourself to then grow durably over the long term," Figma's finance chief, Praveer Melwani, told CNBC in an interview on Wednesday.
The number of weekly users working at organizations that spend over $10,000 on Figma who used AI credits increased by almost 50% during the quarter, Figma said in the statement. The share of work the company's own AI model performs doubled, and the rate of people undoing AI-generated work has fallen .
"If there's certain actions that we can power for our customers at lower latency, lower cost, or similar quality to third party, we're open to that as well," Melwani said.
Figma is increasing its focus on cybersecurity, said Dylan Field, Figma's co-founder and CEO. In recent months, AI agents have infiltrated systems at Hugging Face and other companies.
Clients aren't asking Figma to become a security vendor, but the company must scrutinize "the security of all of our vendors right now," Field said.

headline: E.l.f. Beauty posts 51% sales increase, raises full-year guidance
body:
In this article
E.l.f. Beauty on Wednesday blew past Wall Street expectations as it posted a 51% increase in net sales in its second fiscal quarter.
The beauty company said it saw its 31st consecutive quarter of net sales growth, attributing the streak to strong performance across its portfolio. The revenue spike was driven by both retail and e-commerce channels across the U.S. and internationally, the company added.
"The thing I'm most pleased about is we saw strength across our entire portfolio," CEO Tarang Amin told CNBC in an interview. "Every one of our brands contributed strong growth this quarter."
Amin added that E.l.f. is the most-searched brand on TikTok Shop and the No. 2 brand in cosmetics on the platform. The company also said it saw strong results for Rhode, the skincare brand it acquired last year.
The company raised its full fiscal-year guidance following the better-than-anticipated quarter. It now expects net sales in the range of $2 billion to $2.03 billion, compared with a previous range of between $1.94 billion and $1.97 billion. It also upped its adjusted EBITDA projection to a range of $421 million to $427 million from between $401 million and $407 million.
E.l.f. said it now expects adjusted earnings per share for the year to come in between $3.82 and $3.86, exceeding prior guidance of between $3.50 and $3.55 per share. It's also expecting a net income range of $231 million to $233 million, up from a previous range of $212 million to $215 million.
It had already raised its guidance last quarter after outperforming its expectations.
Amin said the company is "very bullish" on the holiday season, expecting high sales through the end of the year.
Here's how the company performed in its second fiscal quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
For the period ended Sept. 30, E.l.f. reported net income of $30.03 million, or 50 cents per share, up significantly from roughly $3 million, or 5 cents per share, the year prior.
Net sales grew 51% to $520.8 million.
E.l.f. also saw significant growth in its international channels, with business up 165%. Amin told CNBC that only 25% of the company's business is outside of the U.S. and that it has a "tremendous opportunity" to build on that momentum.
The company also said its gross margin increased 1.6% during the quarter, including a 0.3% benefit from tariff refunds. Amin previously said the retailer planned to fully reinvest that money into pricing and marketing to continue driving growth.
Though E.l.f. received most of its refunds in its first fiscal quarter, some of those funds flowed through the second quarter, and the company expects to receive a yearly total of around $55 million. Amin told CNBC on Wednesday that the company lowered the price of about 10% of its units by $1 because of the tariff benefits.
"We're seeing great unit momentum based on that," he said.

headline: Qualcomm stock drops 7% on weak earnings forecast as memory shortage weighs on smartphone sales
body:
In this article
Qualcomm reported quarterly results on Wednesday that topped Wall Street estimates, but the chipmaker's earnings forecast came in lighter than expected. The stock slid 7% in extended trading.
Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates:
For the current quarter, Qualcomm said it sees earnings per share of between $2.15 and $2.35 on revenue of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion. Analysts expected earnings per share of $2.27 on revenue of $10.48 billion.
Most of Qualcomm's chip sales come from system-on-chips and modems for smartphones. It's a market that's currently in turmoil as rising memory costs force handset makers to raise prices, hurting demand. Adjusted company revenue fell 7% during from a year earlier.
Qualcomm raised prices in September. Still, handset chip sales during the quarter fell 26% to $5.14 billion, trailing a StreetAccount estimate of $5.21 billion. Qualcomm said it's starting to see sequential growth in the category, and that Android shipments in China have bottomed, even though the company predicts the handset market will be flat in 2027.
Under CEO Cristiano Amon, Qualcomm has tried to turn investor attention to other kinds of chips. The company is looking to enter the fast-growing market for AI data center infrastructure. It had $650 million in data center revenue during the quarter, mostly from customizing and connectivity work, Amon said.
Amon said Qualcomm expects $5 billion in data center revenue in fiscal 2027. He said the company recently signed a customer for optical connectivity and had engaged a global hyperscaler.
"We don't have a demand issue; it's a supply issue," Amon said. "If I had more supply, I would probably be doing better."
Qualcomm also sells chips for cars and other automotive uses. Revenue in that division soared 89% on an annual basis to $1.99 billion, beating StreetAccount expectations of $1.66 billion.
Internet of things revenue includes low-power chips, smart glasses SoCs, laptop chips, as well as the company's bid to provide cellular infrastructure. Earlier on Wednesday, Qualcomm announced a deal to provide technology to SpaceX's cellular buidlout. IoT revenue increased 4% from a year earlier to $1.88 billion, slightly higher than estimates.
Qualcomm's QTL division includes revenue from licensing its intellectual property for 5G and other technologies to other companies. Qualcomm said during the quarter that it had renewed licensing agreements with Apple, Huawei, and Transsion.
"QTL will maintain its scale going forward," Amon said.
QTL revenue sank 7% to $1.3 billion, in line with a StreetAccount estimate.
